title: Sugar restriction in the first 1000 days after conception, and long-term respiratory health: a quasi-experiment study.
ehr_evidence: We used the cessation of the United Kingdom's sugar rationing in September 1953 as a quasi-experiment, comparing 58,670 UK Biobank participants born 1951–1956 exposed to varying durations of early-life sugar restriction.
summary: In a quasi-experimental study of 58,670 UK Biobank participants born 1951–1956, early-life sugar rationing during the first 1000 days after conception was associated with lower risks of asthma and COPD and improved adult lung function.
key_findings: Early-life sugar rationing (in utero plus 1–2 y) was associated with lower asthma risk (HR 0.75; 95% CI 0.61, 0.91) and lower COPD risk (HR 0.73; 95% CI 0.62, 0.88), with longer exposure conferring greater protection.
No significant association was found for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (HR 0.72; 95% CI 0.46, 1.13; P for trend 0.145).
Sugar rationing delayed disease onset by up to 3.62 y for asthma, 2.85 y for COPD, and 2.74 y for IPF (in utero plus 1–2 y exposure).
Sugar rationing improved lung function: FEV1% predicted increased by 6.03 (95% CI 2.87, 9.13), FVC% by 5.88 (95% CI 3.30, 8.46), and FEV1/FVC ratio by 0.045 (95% CI 0.011, 0.079).
Type 2 diabetes and hypertension jointly mediated 18.2% of the association between sugar rationing and lung disease risk, while birth weight contributed only 1.6%.
Placebo outcomes (influenza and herpes zoster) showed no significant associations, with HR estimates close to 1.
In validation cohorts (UKB internal control, HRS, ELSA), birth period had no significant association with lung disease incidence.
captured_features: Age, sex, race, place of birth, birth month
Smoking status, pack-years, alcohol consumption, physical activity (MET min/wk)
Cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, digestive/kidney/liver diseases
Parental lung disease, maternal smoking around birth, breastfeeding status
Polygenic risk score (PRS) for IPF, COPD, asthma
FEV1%, FVC%, FEV1/FVC ratio, PEF from spirometry
ICD-10 codes for asthma (J45), COPD (J44), IPF (J84.1)
Dates of disease diagnosis, hospitalization, and death
study_design: Quasi-experimental (event-study/regression-discontinuity design based on UK sugar rationing cessation), with Cox proportional hazards and parametric (Gompertz) survival models, validated across external cohorts
population: 58,670 UK Biobank participants born October 1951–March 1956, aged 40–70 at recruitment, predominantly White, UK-based; validated in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (UK) and Health and Retirement Study (US)
exposure_domain: Dietary/nutritional (early-life sugar restriction via national sugar rationing policy during the first 1000 days after conception)
limitations: Exposure was a proxy based on birth period relative to sugar rationing policy; actual individual-level sugar intake was not measured.
Unmeasured confounding or secular trends, including improvements in disease detection, cannot be fully excluded.
Right censoring and lack of prestudy mortality data may introduce survivor bias.
UK Biobank is not nationally representative and is predominantly White, limiting generalizability.
Early-life variables (birth weight, maternal smoking, breastfeeding) were collected via adult self-report and may be subject to recall error.
London data used as a proxy for nationwide air pollution exposure.
Median-based PRS grouping may not reflect true genetic risk distribution.
data_availability_statement: The data are accessible through a public, open-access repository. Data from the UKB, ELSA, and HRS are available to researchers on request.
